content.overview: Assault is an intentional act creating reasonable apprehension of immediate unlawful force; battery is the intentional and direct application of unlawful force without lawful justification. Both protect bodily integrity.
content.glance: Assault is an intentional act creating reasonable apprehension of immediate unlawful force; battery is the intentional and direct application of unlawful force without lawful justification. Both protect bodily integrity.
content.study: Assault is an intentional act creating reasonable apprehension of immediate unlawful force; battery is the intentional and direct application of unlawful force without lawful justification. Both protect bodily integrity.\n\nTrespass to the person developed as a direct-action branch protecting bodily autonomy. Assault focuses on apprehension; battery on actual unlawful contact. Consent, ordinary implied contact and lawful authority may justify conduct. The distinction matters because assault can exist without battery and vice versa.

sections.heading: Provenance, Legislative Objective & Doctrinal Foundations
sections.body: Trespass to the person developed as a direct-action branch protecting bodily autonomy. Assault focuses on apprehension; battery on actual unlawful contact. Consent, ordinary implied contact and lawful authority may justify conduct. The distinction matters because assault can exist without battery and vice versa.

sections.heading: Textual Anatomy, Provisos & Statutory Deconstruction
sections.body: There is no general Indian tort statute codifying assault and battery. Common-law principles apply subject to Indian statutes and constitutional protections. Minor unlawful touching can be actionable even without serious injury.

sections.heading: Mandatory Proving Ingredients & Essential Elements
sections.body: Assault: intentional act or gesture, reasonable apprehension and immediacy of unlawful force. Battery: intentional or legally attributable direct application of unlawful force without consent or justification.

sections.heading: Evidentiary Burdens under BSA 2023 (ss. 104–106 & s. 63)
sections.body: Witnesses, CCTV, medical records and contemporaneous complaints may prove the act and context. Assault does not require physical injury; battery requires unlawful contact.

sections.heading: Procedural Roadmap, Competent Forum & Limitation Act Checkpoints
sections.body: The claim is ordinarily civil and may coexist with criminal proceedings. Plead the act, lack of consent or justification and any damage. Limitation must be checked under the applicable civil regime.

examples.title: Illustration 1 — Doctrine Satisfied
examples.body: Assault can exist without contact; battery concerns unlawful physical contact and does not necessarily require serious injury. The claimant must still prove the remaining ingredients on the civil standard.

examples.title: Illustration 2 — Boundary Defect
examples.body: Assault protects against apprehension of imminent unlawful force and does not require bodily injury. A court should not infer liability from the label alone.
